title: Buying what you cannot taste first
bodyMd:
Extra-virgin olive oil looks, on the shelf, much like every other oil in a green bottle. Yet its quality depends on things a buyer cannot see: when the olives were picked, how quickly they were pressed, whether the oil was stretched with cheaper stock. A shopper can discover the difference only after paying, and often not even then, since a faded flavour is easily blamed on the kitchen rather than the bottle.

Economists have long understood what such a market does. If buyers cannot tell good oil from mediocre oil, they will offer a price that reflects the average quality they expect, and they will discount every bottle accordingly. A careful producer, whose oil costs more to make than that average price repays, is then paid less than the oil is worth. Some such producers stop making the good oil; others leave the market altogether. Average quality falls, buyers become more suspicious, and the price they offer falls again. Nobody chose this outcome. It follows from the fact that the seller knows something the buyer does not.

Cooperatives in southern Italy have tried several remedies. The most common is a tasting panel that grades each season's oil, together with a label that reports the grade. A label does not make the oil better, but it turns a private fact into a public one, and buyers will pay for a fact they can check in a way they will not pay for a promise. Some cooperatives also print the harvest date and the name of the mill, so that a disappointed customer can blame a mill rather than a whole region.

The remedy has a price of its own, and it is not paid equally. Panels must be paid, samples must be tested, and the paperwork favours those who can afford someone to complete it. A large producer spreads these costs over a great many bottles; a family with two hundred trees cannot. In several districts, the result has been that certification raised the average price of good oil while reducing the number of independent producers who sell it. Whether shoppers are better off depends on whether they value certainty more than variety, a question the label cannot answer for them.
accessibilityText: A four-paragraph economics passage of about 370 words titled "Buying what you cannot taste first". The first paragraph says the quality of extra-virgin olive oil depends on things a buyer cannot see, such as picking date, pressing speed and blending with cheaper oil, so a shopper often cannot judge quality even after buying. The second paragraph explains that when buyers cannot tell good oil from mediocre oil they offer a price based on average expected quality and discount every bottle; careful producers are paid less than their oil is worth, some stop or leave, average quality falls, and prices fall again, because the seller knows something the buyer does not. The third paragraph describes southern Italian cooperatives' remedies: a tasting panel and a label reporting the grade, which turns a private fact into a public one, and sometimes the harvest date and mill name so that a mill, not a region, is blamed. The fourth paragraph says the remedy has costs that fall unevenly, favouring large producers; in several districts certification raised the average price of good oil and reduced the number of independent producers, and whether shoppers are better off depends on whether they value certainty over variety.
